construction.quote: The RSC provision purports to provide landlords of rent-stabilized units a remedy to deal with holdover tenants that is expressly precluded by Real Property Law § 232-c.

As such, the parties essentially entered into new, monthly leaseholds each month, all of which commenced and ended after the HSTPA was already in effect, including the landlord's obligations regarding the return or withholding of security deposits.
shall apply to any lease or rental agreement or renewal of a lease or rental agreement entered into on or after such date.

atoms.reasoning: Samson (Appellate Division, Second Department) holds that RPL 232-c governs a stabilized tenant who holds over without signing the offered renewal, so the owner's acceptance of rent creates a month-to-month tenancy and nothing else. Case (Appellate Term, Second Department, binding on Civil Court in Kings, Queens and Richmond) treats that tenancy as a renewal entered into for the HSTPA effective-date clause, whose wording c.436 s.2 repeats. Bogom-Shanon (Civil Court, New York County) reaches the same result by treating each month as a new leasehold. No Appellate Term, First Department or Appellate Division decision holds otherwise, so the rule is the same in all five counties. The c.436 sponsor memo states that the act extends these protections to stabilized tenants (NY:L2025-c436-memo-gap), which agrees with this reading.

atoms.instrument: NYC Housing Maintenance Code 27-2013 with RSC 2520.6(r), DHCR Fact Sheet #28 and the damages rule
atoms.provision: Allocation of repainting at move-out (HMC 27-2013(b)(2); Bohl v Poffenbarger, App Term 2d Dept 2018)
atoms.condition: A departing tenant of an NYC multiple dwelling or one- or two-family dwelling (stabilized, rent-controlled or market) leaves walls that need repainting.
atoms.effect: Repainting needed because of ordinary occupancy (faded or dirty paint, scuffs, small picture-hanging holes, paint at the end of its cycle) is ordinary wear and tear and the owner's cost: in a multiple dwelling the owner must repaint every three years (NYC:HMC-27-2013(b)(2)), and in a one- or two-family dwelling whenever needed to keep surfaces sanitary (NYC:HMC-27-2013(a)); painting is a required service for stabilized units (NYC:RSC-2520.6(r)(1)) and an essential service included in the maximum rent for controlled units. Nothing for it may be deducted or billed. A painting charge is lawful only for damage beyond ordinary wear and tear that the owner proves (e.g. tenant-applied colors or wallcoverings needing extra coats or primer, burns, tenant-caused smoke or water staining, holes beyond picture hanging), in the reasonable cost of the extra work that damage requires beyond the repainting the owner owes at that time. A contractor bill for painting and spackling alone does not prove damage beyond wear and tear. In a stabilized unit a lease 'painting fee' is prohibited outright (NYC:RS-FEE-vs-DAMAGES). HPD's power to order a tenant to repaint (NYC:HMC-27-2013(c)) operates during the tenancy and gives the owner no separate move-out charge. In a one- or two-family dwelling a written lease may allocate repainting to the tenant (NYC:HMC-27-2005(c)-1-2-family-allocation); the tenant's failure to repaint is then a separate lease claim at reasonable cost, never kept from the deposit where it only cures wear and tear.
atoms.quote: the bill merely states window cleaning, painting and spackling, and carpet cleaning, which, without more, is insufficient to establish a condition going beyond ordinary wear and tear.

construction.quote: (2) Repaint or re-cover the walls and ceilings with wallpaper or other acceptable wall covering every three years, and more often when required by contract or other provisions of law.

The owner of a one- or two-family dwelling shall keep the premises in good repair, and shall be responsible for compliance with the provisions of this code, except to the extent otherwise agreed between such owner and any tenant of such dwelling by lease or other contract in writing, or except insofar as responsibility for compliance with this code is imposed upon the tenant alone.

atoms.reasoning: The Housing Maintenance Code puts periodic repainting on the owner, and the rent regulations fold painting into the services the regulated rent pays for, so repainting from normal occupancy is not a loss the tenant caused. The Appellate Term, Second Department (Bohl; Blansett, 2d, 11th and 13th Districts) requires the owner to prove damage beyond wear and tear before a painting cost is recoverable, and Gable puts the reasonable cost on the owner. Damages compensate only the loss the tenant caused, so the recoverable amount is the extra work beyond the repaint the owner owes anyway.

atoms.condition: The owner (or its agent or assignee) sues a former stabilized tenant for rent arrears or damages, and the tenant has not already elected to proceed before DHCR on the same overcharge.
atoms.effect: The tenant may raise the overcharge as a defense and counterclaim in that action without first going to DHCR. The court determines the legal regulated rent, awards the overcharge for up to six years before the claim (treble if willful, 26-516(a); interest, costs and attorney's fees, 26-516(a)(4)), nets it against the owner's proven claim and may give the tenant judgment for any excess. Where the tenant chose DHCR, DHCR decides and its order is enforceable as a judgment once the tenant is out of possession (NYC:RSC-2526.7(i)(7)).
atoms.quote: a rent overcharge claim, including a claim that the rent amount is illegal under the applicable state and city rent regulations, may be asserted in the Civil Court, either as a primary claim or as a counterclaim, without first being passed upon by the DHCR

construction.quote: (2) A complaint under this subdivision may be filed with the state division of housing and community renewal or in a court of competent jurisdiction at any time, however any recovery of overcharge penalties shall be limited to the six years preceding the complaint.
recognition of concurrent jurisdiction with respect to overcharge claims “subject to the tenant’s choice of forum

atoms.reasoning: The statute lets the tenant bring the overcharge claim in court at any time. The Appellate Division, Second Department holds that Civil Court hears it as a counterclaim and reduces the owner's judgment by it, and DHCR's 2023 rulemaking recognizes concurrent jurisdiction subject to the tenant's choice of forum. So the owner's balance claim and the tenant's overcharge claim are decided and netted in one action unless the tenant has chosen DHCR.

atoms.condition: The owner prepares the final account of a departing stabilized tenant and the rent history shows amounts collected above the legal regulated rent within the six years before the account.
atoms.effect: Rent owed may be computed only at the legal regulated rent (NYC:RSC-2525.1). Amounts collected above it are overcharges for which the owner is liable to the tenant (treble unless the owner proves they were not willful). The owner may credit them against the tenant's balance on the final statement or refund them. A voluntary adjustment or refund made before an overcharge complaint is filed and served may be weighed on willfulness; one made after may not.
atoms.quote: After a complaint of rent overcharge has been filed and served on an owner, the voluntary adjustment of the rent and/or the voluntary tender of a refund of rent overcharges shall not be considered by the division of housing and community renewal or a court of competent jurisdiction as evidence that the overcharge was not willful.

construction.quote: It shall be unlawful, regardless of any contract, lease or other obligation heretofore or hereafter entered into, for any person to demand or receive any rent for any housing accommodation in excess of the legal regulated rent,

atoms.reasoning: By barring post-complaint refunds as evidence of good faith, the statute presupposes that an owner may adjust the rent and refund before a complaint, and that such a refund bears on willfulness. The owner's liability runs to the same tenant who owes the balance, so crediting it on the final statement settles both debts between the same parties.

atoms.condition: A tenant of an NYC unit moves out voluntarily and leaves belongings.

atoms.condition: The stabilized tenant of record permanently vacates or dies, and a family member who meets 2523.5(b)(1) remains and claims succession (or the owner accepts it).
atoms.effect: The tenancy continues: the successor takes the renewal lease on the same terms and conditions, including the deposit already held as security. The settlement chain does not start at the tenant of record's departure: no refund, statement or 14-day clock runs, because the premises have not been vacated. The deposit stays in trust as the depositor's money and secures the continuing tenancy; it is settled when the successor tenancy ends. At that settlement the refund goes to the holder of the depositor's right: the person who paid it (or that person's estate) unless that person assigned it to the successor; any new or top-up deposit the successor paid is the successor's.

atoms.reasoning: Succession gives the family member the renewal lease, and the renewal must repeat the expired lease's terms, which include the deposit; the tenancy is continued, not ended. The statutory return duty is triggered by the tenant having vacated the premises, which does not happen while the successor occupies them. GOL 7-103(1) keeps the deposit the money of the person who made it, so ownership of the refund does not pass to the successor without an assignment.

atoms.condition: A person collects or tries to collect from a natural person a balance left by a residential tenancy in NYC (rent, damage, charges).
atoms.effect: That is 'collection of consumer debts' under 20-700: a tenant's obligations for the home he or she rented are debts primarily for personal, household or family purposes. DCWP's debt-collection rules made under 20-700 reach it: until 2026-12-31 the current 6 RCNY 5-77 practice rules bind every individual who regularly collects such balances, including the owner's or manager's staff (NYC:RCNY6-5-76-debt-collector); from 2027-01-01 the SHIELD Rule also binds the owner or manager itself once debt collection procedures begin (NYC:SHIELD-5-76-debt-collector, NYC:DCWP-FAQ-procedures-trigger).
atoms.quote: c. Consumer goods, services, credit and debts. As used in section 20-700 of this subchapter and subdivisions a and b of this section, goods, services, credit and debts which are primarily for personal, household or family purposes.

construction.quote: Debt. The term "debt" means any obligation or alleged obligation of a consumer to pay money arising out of a transaction in which the money, property, insurance, or services which are the subject of the transaction are primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, whether or not such obligation has been reduced to judgment.
We therefore hold that, under the FDCPA, back rent is debt.
Therefore, regardless of who sends out a rent demand notice, unpaid rent falls within the more general definition of consumer debt.

atoms.reasoning: The Consumer Protection Law defines consumer debts by purpose alone, and a tenant's obligation for his or her home is household in purpose. DCWP's rules under 20-700 use the FDCPA's wording for 'debt', which the Second Circuit applied to back rent in Romea, and New York courts read the same wording in CPLR 5004 to cover rent (Allen). No authority read limits the collection limb of 20-700 to credit transactions.

A landlord collecting rent and move-out charges is not one, because a lease is not credit, so the procedure does not bind its staff. A landlord becomes one only if it regularly extends consumer credit payable by agreement in more than four installments or with a finance charge, for example as a regular practice of installment plans for move-out balances (US:15USC1602(g)); its staff then follow the procedure on those accounts. The other current 5-77 practice rules bind the staff as 'debt collectors' either way. From 2027-01-01 the SHIELD validation notice applies once debt collection procedures begin (NYC:SHIELD-5-77(f)(1)).
atoms.quote: (1) Upon acceleration of the unpaid balance of the debt or demand for the full balance due, the following validation procedures shall be followed by debt collectors who are creditors or who are employed by creditors as defined by 15 U.S.C. § 1602(f) (Truth in Lending Act)

construction.quote: Based on the foregoing case law and statutes, this court agrees with plaintiff that a landlord does not "extend credit" when entering into lease agreements with a tenant.
Heiberger’s first ground misconstrues the issue, which is not whether all rent is an extension of credit, but whether back rent is a debt.

atoms.reasoning: A TILA creditor is one who extends consumer credit. A lease grants possession for rent; courts treat back rent as a debt without treating the lease as an extension of credit (Romea; Allen). The current validation clause is limited to creditors so defined, so it does not reach a landlord's staff.

atoms.instrument: NYC Administrative Code
atoms.effective_from: 2022-06-22 (L.L. 2021/169, effective 180 days after it became law on 2021-12-24); applies only to leases entered into on or after that date
atoms.actor: landlord; managing agent; Handoff or collector seeking the amount for the landlord
atoms.condition: An NYC residential lease entered into on or after 2022-06-22 (a renewal lease signed on or after that date is a lease entered into then); the tenant vacated in violation of the lease terms, so the landlord has the RPL 227-e duty to mitigate; the landlord seeks from the tenant, by deduction on the move-out statement, by demand, through a collector or in suit, an amount arising from the vacating other than rent it proves under 227-e.
atoms.effect: The landlord may not recover from the tenant any amount above the fair market cost necessary to prepare the physical condition of the unit for rental. Every other charge for leaving early, whether or not the lease fixes it (a lease-break or early-termination fee, a sum fixed as liquidated damages for vacating, a re-letting, re-rental, broker, advertising, administrative or processing fee, a turnover charge above fair market cost), falls within that ceiling, so none is recovered on top of it by deduction, demand or suit. Rent the landlord proves for the period until the unit is re-let at fair market value or the lease rate, mitigated under RPL 227-e, is outside the ceiling. Whenever the landlord seeks the amount it must give the tenant an itemized list demonstrating the calculation; a statement line or demand without that list does not meet the section. The ceiling creates no charge: preparation costs are recoverable only as state and city law already allow (damage the tenant caused beyond normal wear and tear, NY:GOL-7-108(1-a)(b)-refundable; never the owner's statutory turnover work, NYC:HMC-27-2056.8-lead-turnover, NYC:HMC-27-2017.5-turnover). A tenant who left under a lawful termination right (RPL 227-a, 227-c, SCRA, month-to-month notice) did not breach, so the section does not apply and no vacating charge is owed under those rules. A lease entered into before 2022-06-22 and not renewed since is outside the section (NY:ADJ-lease-break-charge governs it).
judgment_terms: fair market cost necessary to prepare the physical conditions of the premises for rental
amount arising from the vacating versus rent damages
atoms.quote: Where a landlord has a duty to mitigate damages, such landlord may not recover from a tenant any amount in excess of the fair market cost necessary to prepare the physical conditions of the premises for rental. In seeking such amount from a tenant, such landlord must provide an itemized list to such tenant demonstrating the calculation of such amount.

construction.quote: the term "duty to mitigate damages" means the duty of a landlord to mitigate damages pursuant to section 227-e of the real property law.

the new tenant's lease shall, once in effect, terminate the previous tenant's lease and mitigate damages otherwise recoverable against the previous tenant because of such tenant's vacating the premises.
§ 2. This local law shall take effect 180 days after becoming law, provided that it shall apply only to leases entered into on or after such date.

While this duty to mitigate damages is helpful for limiting damages related to lost rent, it does not address other fees that may be imposed when a tenant vacates a residence in violation of lease terms, such as penalties for breaking a lease.

Proposed Int. No. 2312-A would limit the fees that a landlord can recover when a tenant vacates a residence prior to the end of the lease term to the fair market costs necessary to prepare the residence for rental.

These fees could be specified in the lease agreement (e.g. fees for vacating in slower rental months or specific lease break penalties) or imposed by the landlord to alleviate some of the inconvenience (e.g. cleaning and painting fees).

atoms.reasoning: The section's words ('any amount') are read with its definition (the landlord's RPL 227-e duty) and the Council's record. The Housing and Buildings Committee reports on Int. 2312 and 2312-A (2021-11-09 and 2021-11-22) state that 227-e already limits damages for lost rent and that the bill limits the other fees a landlord charges when a tenant leaves in breach, naming lease-break penalties, fees for vacating in slower rental months, and cleaning and painting fees, to the fair market cost of preparing the unit. Mitigated rent damages therefore stay governed by 227-e, and every other vacating charge, lease-fixed or not, falls within the ceiling; a lease-break sum stated as liquidated damages is such a fee. Section 2 of Local Law 169 applies the chapter only to leases entered into on or after its effective date, 2022-06-22. The chapter was renumbered from 26-3301/3302 by L.L. 2023/030 without change. Searches of CourtListener's New York opinions for '26-3402', '26-3302' and 'fair market cost necessary to prepare', and a web search, found no decision construing the section.

atoms.condition: The owner of a dwelling unit gives money or other valuable consideration to a person lawfully entitled to occupy it.

A mutual early-termination agreement in which the owner gives anything of value (cash, a waiver of rent or charges owed, return of more of the deposit than is owed) and the tenant vacates is one; an ordinary move-out at lease end with no inducement is not.

atoms.instrument: NYC Administrative Code
atoms.actor: owner; managing agent; Handoff or anyone acting on the owner's behalf
atoms.condition: Before the tenant has vacated, the owner or someone on its behalf (manager, Handoff) contacts a person lawfully entitled to occupy an NYC dwelling unit, or that person's relative, offering money or other consideration (including a waiver of rent or charges or a larger refund) to induce the person to vacate or surrender or waive occupancy rights (for example an agreed early termination proposed by the owner).
atoms.effect: The owner must, at the first such contact and again at the first contact more than 180 days after its last disclosure, state in writing: the purpose of the contact; that the person may reject the offer and stay; that the person may consult an attorney and may use HPD's ABCs of Housing guide; that the contact is by or for the owner; that the person may refuse such contact in writing, barring it for 180 days; the median asking rent for the community district (with the same bedroom count where HPD reports it); that there is no guarantee of renting a comparable unit at the same rent; and that employment and credit history may affect renting. After a written refusal, no offer may be made to the person or a relative for 180 days unless a court permits it or the person writes asking for offers. No offer may be made while threatening or using obscene language, contacting with abusive frequency or at unusual hours, contacting the person at work without written consent, or knowingly misrepresenting facts. Any of these is harassment, which 27-2005(d) bars; outside a private (one- or two-family) dwelling it is presumed intended to make the person vacate, and the presumption is rebuttable. A tenant who itself asks to end the lease early and negotiates terms is not contacted 'to induce' vacating by the owner's reply to that request.
judgment_terms: to induce such person to vacate
such frequency ... as can reasonably be expected to abuse or harass
atoms.quote: contacting any person lawfully entitled to occupancy of such dwelling unit to offer money or other valuable consideration to induce such person to vacate such dwelling unit or to surrender or waive any rights in relation to such occupancy, unless such owner discloses to such person in writing (i) at the time of the initial contact, and (ii) in the event that contacts continue more than 180 days after the prior written disclosure, at the time of the first contact occurring more than 180 days after the prior written disclosure:

construction.quote: The owner of a dwelling shall not harass any tenants or persons lawfully entitled to occupancy of such dwelling as set forth in paragraph 48 of subdivision a of section 27-2004 of this chapter.

atoms.reasoning: Paragraph 48 defines harassment as an act by or for an owner that causes or is intended to cause a lawful occupant to vacate or surrender rights and that includes a listed act; items f-1 to f-3 list the buyout-contact acts. Section 27-2005(d) forbids the owner to harass. 'Owner' in paragraph 45 includes an agent or anyone in control of the dwelling.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 3, section NYC:ADC 27-2004 (new_rule, major)

atoms.instrument: NYC Administrative Code
atoms.actor: owner; managing agent; Handoff or anyone acting on the owner's behalf
atoms.condition: While a person is still lawfully entitled to occupy an NYC dwelling unit (before surrender or abandonment), the owner or someone acting for it, in connection with ending the tenancy or settling the account: tells the person something false or misleading about the occupancy (e.g. that the lease has ended or must end when Good Cause or another law protects the tenancy, or that rent is owed that is not); starts repeated baseless or frivolous court proceedings; removes the person's belongings; removes the door, disables or changes the lock without giving a key; repeatedly contacts or visits on weekends, legal holidays or outside 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., or in an abusive manner, without the person's written consent to those times; threatens the person based on a protected status (including lawful source of income and domestic-violence victim status); requests documents disclosing citizenship after government ID was given; or does anything barred by the unlawful eviction law (26-521).
atoms.effect: Each such act, when it causes or is intended to cause the person to vacate or surrender or waive occupancy rights, is harassment that the owner may not commit (27-2005(d)); outside a one- or two-family dwelling the intent is presumed, rebuttably. 'Owner' includes the freeholder, lessee, receiver, agent and anyone directly or indirectly in control, so the owner answers for its manager and Handoff. Contacts that law requires or specifically authorizes (the pre-vacate inspection notice, the 14-day statement) are allowed at any time. Once the tenant has surrendered or abandoned the unit it is no longer a person lawfully entitled to occupancy, and collection conduct is governed by the collection rules (US:15USC1692d, NYC:RCNY6-5-77(b)(1)(iv)).
judgment_terms: causes or is intended to cause ... to vacate
manner as can reasonably be expected to abuse or harass
atoms.quote: the term "harassment" shall mean any act or omission by or on behalf of an owner that (i) causes or is intended to cause any person lawfully entitled to occupancy of a dwelling unit to vacate such dwelling unit or to surrender or waive any rights in relation to such occupancy, and

construction.quote: knowingly providing to any person lawfully entitled to occupancy of a dwelling unit false or misleading information relating to the occupancy of such unit;

The term "owner" shall mean and include the owner or owners of the freehold of the premises or lesser estate therein, a mortgagee or vendee in possession, assignee of rents, receiver, executor, trustee, lessee, agent, or any other person, firm or corporation, directly or indirectly in control of a dwelling.

atoms.reasoning: The listed items in paragraph 48 are each harassment when joined with the purpose element; 27-2005(d) bars harassment; paragraph 45 makes agents and anyone in control 'owners'. The authorized-contact carve-out comes from item f-4's proviso for contacts authorized or mandated by law or rule.
atoms.origin: register queue batch 3, section NYC:ADC 27-2004 (new_rule, major)

atoms.instrument: NYC Admin. Code tit. 20 ch. 1 (DCWP licensing, general provisions)
atoms.actor: debt collection agency required to hold a DCWP licence (for Handoff by configuration, NYC:DCA-handoff-principal-purpose; a debt buyer, NYC:DCA-debt-buyer)
atoms.condition: A person that must hold a DCWP licence under Admin. Code title 20 chapter 2 (for this chain, a debt collection agency under 20-489 and 20-490) collects former NYC tenants' balances without the licence.

Sealed premises and devices are released only on payment of all fines and costs and proof of a licence. NYC adds FARE fee disclosure (leases from 2025-06-11) and HMC painting duties. Sweep 2026-09-29: lead turnover work (pre-1960 building) and mold/pest turnover work are the owner's cost; a missing detector is chargeable only within the 27-2045 caps; HPD repair charges are the owner's debt; rent under an HPD receivership or rent levy goes to the receiver or HPD.

C4 NYC unit in a building of fewer than.note: Not automatically unregulated: a fewer-than-6 building can be rent-controlled (pre-1947, 3+ unit or continuous pre-1953 occupancy in 1-2 family houses) or stabilized via J-51/421-a. If stabilized or controlled, the NYC deposit rules require an interest-bearing account even though GOL 7-103(2-a) does not (below 6 units). Sweep 2026-09-29: a rented pre-1960 one- or two-family house is covered by the lead turnover duty; a rented cellar room is lawful only as an ADU with a certificate of occupancy, but rent stays recoverable in a house of two families at most.

C5a Lease signed before HSTPA (before 20.note: For NYC, the dates that matter are 2019-06-14 (end of deregulation; status of the unit) and, for stabilized units, the lease/renewal date against 2025-11-15 (which 7-107 applies). A long-tenured stabilized tenant may still have a deposit above one month.

C5b Lease signed after HSTPA.note: Stabilized: a lease or renewal entered into on or after 2025-11-15 brings amended 7-107 (14-day statement, forfeiture). One entered 2019-07-14 to 2025-11-14 does not: 7-108 excludes stabilized units, so the non-statutory rule applies (NY:COMMONLAW-deposit-return; NY:ADJ-RS-pre2025-7108-inapplicable). An unsigned-renewal holdover across 2025-11-15 is under amended 7-107 if the owner accepted rent into a month beginning on or after 2025-11-15, and under its last signed lease otherwise (NYC:RS-HOLDOVER-rent-accepted, NYC:RS-HOLDOVER-no-rent-accepted). Leases from 2025-06-11 also carry the FARE fee disclosure; an undisclosed move-out service fee may not be charged (NYC:FARE-moveout-service-fee).

C6 Early termination.note: Stabilized/market: NYC adds no early-termination right (RSC 2522.5(f) on early vacancy was repealed 2023-11-08); state RPL 227-e mitigation governs rent after vacating (NY worker); the owner cannot hold a holdover tenant to a deemed new term (Samson). Rent-controlled: 30 days' registered/certified-mail notice, else lost rent up to one month (2204.1(d)). Rent claimed for post-vacatur months is capped at the legal regulated/maximum rent. Voucher households: notify HRA/DSS within 5 business days and return subsidy for months not occupied; SCRIE/DRIE: notify DOF/agency within 30 days.

C7 Damage above the deposit that needs a.note: NYC adds no contractor extension to the state 14-day clock. The excess is pursued as a damages claim: no legal fees on the statement without a court order; every amount must trace to the lease or law; in a stabilized unit a fixed 'damage' or 'cleaning' fee is an overcharge while proven damage is recoverable. The balance is a consumer debt, so DCWP's collection rules apply to whoever collects it; a licence is needed only by a collector whose principal business is collecting others' debts, or a debt buyer (NYC:DCA-* atoms); from 2027-01-01 the SHIELD Rule makes a landlord collecting its own debt a 'debt collector' once collection procedures start (5-day mailed validation notice with itemization). A stabilized tenant's overcharge claim is netted against the balance in the owner's action. Before suing for rent, an owner required to register with HPD registers; otherwise the court may stay the rent claim. Sweep 2026-09-29: statutory turnover work (lead, mold, pests) is not tenant damage; HPD charges are not passed through; detectors within the caps.

C8 Multiple tenants, one leaving.note: Only lease-named tenants owe the owner the full legal rent; occupants are not tenants. If the stabilized tenant of record leaves and a qualifying family member stays, succession continues the tenancy on the same terms, the deposit stays as security and no settlement runs until the successor tenancy ends; the refund then belongs to the depositor unless assigned (NYC:RS-SUCCESSION-tenancy-continues). If succession fails, the tenant of record's settlement runs when the owner regains possession (NYC:RS-SUCCESSION-claim-fails). Payee among co-tenants: NY:ADJ-cotenants-payee.

C9 No forwarding address.note: No NYC rule on delivering the statement or refund to an unknown address; state delivery and unclaimed-funds rules govern (NY worker). The deposit and any held interest remain the tenant's trust money. Agency notices (HRA, DOF) are still due on learning of the departure.

C10 Building sold mid-tenancy.note: Deposit transfer and buyer liability are state law. NYC adds the buyer's DHCR notice duties (30 days RS; 15 days RC) and the address notice to tenants; a judicial-sale buyer may lack pre-sale rent records, which bears on proving the legal rent in the final account. Sweep 2026-09-29: an HPD receiver collects accrued and accruing rents; an HPD rent levy redirects rent to HPD.

C11 Abandoned property.note: No NYC rule governs belongings after a voluntary move-out; the marshals' rules cover only evictions and legal possessions. State rule: belongings stay the tenant's, no holding for rent, disposal only on proof of abandonment; moving and storage costs may be charged against the deposit where the retention list allows (NYC:ABANDONED-city-layer).

C12 Statement due on a weekend or holida.note: No NYC-local time-computation rule reaches the deposit statement (Admin. Code searched); GCN 20 and 25-a (NY worker) govern. DHCR service rules (2527.9, 2209.1) apply only to DHCR proceedings.

VA-only cases (utility withholding; dama.note: Not NYC. Closest NYC analogue: HRA security vouchers in lieu of cash deposits (NYC:RCNY68-10-14(c), NYC:RCNY31-5-06(a)(1); claims: NYC:HRA-voucher-claim-window, NYC:DSS-SOTA-voucher-claim).

X1 Voucher-secured or HPD-escrowed depos.note: Voucher: no cash deposit to refund; the landlord claims against HRA/DSS within three months after the tenant vacates, with sworn, notarized proof, up to one month's rent (SOTA: rent only after the first year). HPD escrow: HPD refunds principal and interest to the tenant on the owner's certification; the owner has no draw on the escrow and pursues arrears or damages against the tenant, unless the building's regulatory agreement provides a procedure (NYC:HPD-ESCROW-no-owner-draw, NYC:HPD-ESCROW-regulatory-agreement).

C14 Balance handed to a collector.note: City side of C14: DCWP licence for a collection agency; rent under an HPD receivership or levy is not the owner's to hand off; HPD repair charges are never part of the tenant's balance. A DCWP-licensed collector that sues pleads its licence (CPLR 3015(e)).
